metric_rationale: In this specific experimental design, Take The Best (TTB) will systematically choose the option with the highest-validity discriminating cue, which on the critical conflict trials (trials 1-6) happens to be the option with the *smaller* total number of positive features. The Weighted Additive (WADD) model, being compensatory, will consistently favor the option with the *larger* total number of positive features because the coalition of lower-validity cues outweighs the single highest-validity cue. By calculating the proportion of trials where the subject chooses the option with fewer positive features, we expect a value near 0.75 for TTB (matching on 6 out of 8 unique trials) and near 0.0 for WADD (which always picks the option with more positive features in this design).

Calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the experimental design explicitly pits a single high-validity cue against a coalition of multiple lower-validity cues on 8 out of 10 trial types, TTB and WADD will make opposing predictions for the majority of the experiment. TTB simulated data will yield a very high proportion (near 1.0, minus noise), whereas WADD simulated data will yield a very low proportion (as the compensatory coalitions will outweigh the single top cue).

This metric isolates the critical trials where Tallying and WADD make diametrically opposed predictions. In these trials, one option has 3 low-validity features while the competing option has 2 high-validity features. Tallying simply counts features and strongly prefers the 3-feature option. WADD weighs features by validity and generally prefers the 2-feature option. The metric computes the proportion of choices that align with Tallying's prediction on these specific trials.

The design includes a crucial reversal between Trial 2 (A=[1,1,0,0,0] vs B=[0,0,1,1,1]) and Trial 3 (A=[0,0,1,1,1] vs B=[1,1,0,0,0]). In Trial 2, Tallying counts 2 positive cues for A and 3 for B, thus predicting a preference for B. WADD, however, values the two highest-validity cues of A (1.0 + 0.8 = 1.8) more than the three lower-validity cues of B (0.6 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.6), predicting a preference for A. Trial 3 is the exact opposite. By computing the difference in the probability of choosing Option A between Trial 2 and Trial 3, we expect a strongly negative value for Tallying (which prefers B then A) and a strongly positive value for WADD (which prefers A then B).

Pure Tallying predicts that the probability of choosing the option with more features depends entirely on the difference in feature counts. In this design, 7 out of the 8 unique trial pairs have a feature count difference of exactly 1. Therefore, Pure Tallying dictates that the true probability of choosing the option with more features is mathematically identical across all 7 of these trial pairs. Any variation in a subject's choice proportions across these 7 pairs is purely due to binomial sampling noise, resulting in a tightly bounded, very small variance. Soft Threshold Tallying, however, down-weights low-validity features. Consequently, its true probability of choosing the option with more features will vary drastically across these 7 pairs (depending on whether the extra features happen to be high or low validity). By computing the within-subject sample variance of the choice proportions across these 7 trial pairs, we obtain a metric that is structurally constrained to be near zero for Pure Tallying, but significantly positive for Soft Threshold Tallying, perfectly isolating the divergence.

Equal Weight Tallying evaluates Trials 4 and 8 as perfect ties (3 vs 3 features), predicting P(A)=0.5 for both, making `P(A|T4) - P(A|T8)` exactly 0 in expectation. Soft Threshold Tallying behaves identically to Tallying for roughly 90% of its parameter space (when the threshold is too low to mask out features), which washes out mean-based contrasts. However, for the ~10% of subjects with a high threshold, STT strongly prefers A in Trial 4 and B in Trial 8, pushing this difference toward +1.0. By evaluating the maximum of this difference across subjects on the pooled data, we explicitly target the right tail of the STT parameter distribution. Tallying will yield a low maximum driven purely by binomial noise, while STT will yield a massive spike near 1.0, cleanly breaking the models apart.

This metric computes the total count difference in choosing Option A between tie trials where the lexicographic tie-breaker favors A and those where it favors B. By computing the unnormalized sum rather than the mean, the metric naturally scales with the number of trials evaluated. On a single subject's slice, it returns a moderately variable count difference. However, when applied to the fully pooled DataFrame, it aggregates the signal across all subjects simultaneously, producing a massive point estimate. Under pure Tallying, this count difference is expected to be exactly 0 (with binomial noise). Under Lexicographic Tie-Breaking, subjects consistently favor the lexicographic winner, leading to a strong positive sum. This sum-based aggregation effectively amplifies the overall effect size on the pooled dataset while maintaining zero-mean for the null model, maximizing the statistical power to discriminate the theories.

This metric isolates trials where the two options have an equal number of positive features (tally ties). On these trials, Pure Tallying predicts subjects will guess randomly (50% accuracy relative to any tie-breaking rule). In contrast, Tallying with Lexicographic Tie-Breaking predicts subjects will systematically choose the option with the highest validity differing feature. By calculating the proportion of choices on tied trials that align with the lexicographic tie-breaker, the metric cleanly separates the two theories (yielding ~0.5 for Pure Tallying and >0.5 for Lexicographic Tie-Breaking).

This metric isolates the specific trials (Trial 1 and Trial 2) where the Tallying model and the Weighted Additive (WADD) model make diametrically opposed predictions. In these trials, one option has more total features (favored by Tallying) but the other option has fewer features with significantly higher validities (favored by WADD). By calculating the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying prediction on these specific conflict trials, we obtain a metric that will be very high (~1) for agents using Tallying and very low (~0) for agents using WADD.

The metric targets the subset of trials where Weighted Additive (WADD) and Tallying make strict, diametrically opposed predictions (Trials 1 and 2). On these trials, one option has a higher weighted sum of validities, while the other option has a strictly greater number of positive features. The metric computes the proportion of decisions that align with the WADD prediction. Data generated by the WADD model will yield a value close to 1, whereas data generated by Tallying will yield a value close to 0, ensuring maximum discrimination with minimal per-subject variance.
